title: CCUS investment: what will separate the projects that move forward? | Wood Mackenzie
gist: Takeaways from Wood Mackenzie's October 2026 CCUS Conference argue the sector is entering a selective phase where capital flows to de-risked projects with secured storage, proven capture tech and durable revenues. AI/data-centre power demand is a tailwind but does not by itself make projects investable.

insights.claim: CCUS is entering a more selective phase in which the key question is which projects reach final investment decision and commercial operation, not how many are announced.
insights.speaker: Linda Htein
insights.so_what: Announced pipeline size is a poor signal; screen for FID-readiness.
insights.quote: Carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS) is entering a more selective phase.

insights.claim: Capital is increasingly concentrated around CCUS projects where development risk is already reduced: secured and permitted storage, experienced partners, proven capture technology, clear cost visibility and durable revenues.
insights.speaker: Linda Htein
insights.so_what: Favors developers with permitted storage and experienced partners; early-stage ambitious projects face funding scarcity.

insights.claim: Execution is becoming as important as ambition for CCUS developers, and the next phase will be defined by how effectively individual projects address risk across the value chain rather than by pipeline count.
insights.speaker: Linda Htein
insights.so_what: Expect attrition in the project pipeline and a winner-takes-most dynamic for executable projects.
insights.quote: execution is becoming as important as ambition
insights.locator: What will determine the next phase of CCUS?

insights.claim: Access to transport and permitted storage, clear carbon-accounting frameworks, durable policy support, stronger demand signals and partnerships with complementary expertise will determine which CCUS projects progress.
insights.speaker: Linda Htein
insights.so_what: A checklist for diligence on CCUS developers and infrastructure plays.
insights.locator: Access to transport and permitted storage

insights.claim: The conference drew nearly 300 participants from more than 150 organisations across the CCUS value chain, and its three standout themes were reliable power, reducing the cost of proven capture technology, and building durable revenue models.
insights.speaker: Linda Htein
insights.so_what: Indicates where industry attention and spending priorities are heading.

insights.claim: Rapid growth in electricity demand from AI and data centres is putting the power sector increasingly at the centre of the CCS opportunity, as hyperscalers seek reliable, lower-carbon power.
insights.speaker: Linda Htein
insights.so_what: Gas-with-CCS could be a niche source of firm low-carbon power for AI load, but only for de-risked projects.

insights.claim: Hyperscaler demand creates an opportunity for CCS but demand alone does not make projects investable.
insights.speaker: Linda Htein
insights.so_what: Cautions against assuming AI power demand automatically funds CCS projects.
insights.quote: demand alone does not make projects investable

insights.claim: For post-combustion capture, the central challenge is increasingly economics and scale rather than technological feasibility.
insights.speaker: Linda Htein
insights.so_what: Value creation is in cost reduction and scaling rather than novel technology breakthroughs.

insights.claim: Amine-based capture is commercially established and a preferred option for many projects, but its costs are high and are being pressured further by energy market volatility, inflation and higher raw-material prices.
insights.speaker: Linda Htein
insights.so_what: Input-cost inflation erodes project returns for incumbent capture technology.

insights.claim: Alternative capture technologies could ultimately lower costs but many still need commercial-scale demonstration and policy support before developers and investors will deploy them widely.
insights.speaker: Linda Htein
insights.so_what: Next-generation capture vendors face a long path to bankability.

insights.claim: In the interim the industry is pursuing standardisation, project replication and greater supply-chain maturity to improve capture economics, but these gains depend on projects actually progressing.
insights.speaker: Linda Htein
insights.so_what: Cost-down is a function of build volume, creating a chicken-and-egg problem.
insights.locator: In the meantime, the industry is focusing

insights.claim: Permitting and regulatory hurdles plus retrofit and integration complexity continue to constrain CCUS deployment, and in harder-to-abate sectors economics can stay challenging even as project experience grows.
insights.speaker: Linda Htein
insights.so_what: Industrial retrofit CCUS has slower, riskier timelines than greenfield projects.

insights.claim: CCS is unlikely to become a fully market-driven industry in the near term, so many projects will continue to depend on policy support and multiple revenue sources.
insights.speaker: Linda Htein
insights.so_what: CCS returns remain exposed to policy risk; subsidy changes are the key swing factor.
insights.quote: CCS is unlikely to become a fully market-driven industry in the near term.
insights.locator: The result is that CCS is unlikely

insights.claim: The US 45Q tax credit has been important to CCUS project economics, but because incentives are time limited developers must plan for viability over much longer operating lives once incentives evolve or expire.
insights.speaker: Linda Htein
insights.so_what: Post-45Q revenue stacking is the key long-term valuation question for US CCUS assets.
insights.locator: Support mechanisms such as the US 45Q

insights.claim: Durable CCUS revenue will likely come from combining several sources of value, including carbon markets, environmental attribute certificates and government and market-driven incentives, rather than relying on one.
insights.speaker: Linda Htein
insights.so_what: Revenue-stacking capability is a differentiator among developers.
insights.locator: Carbon markets and environmental attribute certificates

insights.claim: The voluntary carbon market could bridge towards more mature compliance and commercial markets for CCUS, though questions remain over the depth and durability of its demand.
insights.speaker: Linda Htein
insights.so_what: Voluntary credit demand is an uncertain support for CCUS cash flows.
